articles.title: AWOL Vision Opens Pre-Orders for LuxVision: World's First Optical-Shift 4K 120Hz Projector
articles.text:
Saturday, October 17th 2026
AWOL Vision Opens Pre-Orders for LuxVision: World's First Optical-Shift 4K 120Hz Projector
AWOL Vision, a global home entertainment brand delivering immersive audiovisual experiences through large-format displays, home cinema technology, and connected entertainment, announced that the AWOL LuxVision, first unveiled at IFA 2026, is now officially available for pre-order. Customers can reserve LuxVision with a $100 / €100 / £100 deposit to unlock exclusive Super Early Bird Benefits ahead of its official launch.
This world's first UST projector with optional lens shift is designed to adapt to the changing ways people use their big screens, delivering a tailored experience for every scenario. The big screen is no longer just for movie nights. Gaming is moving toward higher frame rates, sports fans are following multiple live events at once, and home theaters are becoming a more integrated part of everyday living spaces.Built for Every Big Screen Moment
Today's gamers expect a big screen to be just as fast and responsive as the games they play. Size alone isn't enough when the experience can't keep pace with the action. LuxVision delivers 4K at 120 Hz from input to output, bringing sharper, smoother motion to the giant screen. With 1 ms input lag at 4K 120 Hz, VRR and ALLM, gameplay stays fast and responsive. 6,000 ISO lumens help maintain vivid images even in real-home lighting, while Dolby Vision Gaming further enhances compatible titles. Together, these features bring the high refresh rates, brightness and low latency of modern gaming to a truly cinematic scale.
Bringing that big screen experience home means making it work with the space you already have. Lens shift has long given long-throw projectors more flexibility in installation, but UST owners haven't had the same option. LuxVision changes that with the industry's first vertical lens shift for UST, allowing users to move the image vertically within a 142-152% offset range without cropping, scaling, or sacrificing true 4K detail. This makes it easier to install, fine-tune, or upgrade a UST setup without having to reposition the screen or replace existing furniture. Combined with its 0.18:1 ultra-short-throw ratio, LuxVision can project a 120-inch image from just 7.5 inches away, bringing a giant screen into the room while taking up remarkably little space.
And all that big screen can do more than show one thing at a time. For sports fans, that means no longer having to choose between games when several big matchups are happening at once. With LuxVision's optional Multiview upgrade, users can connect multiple wired and wireless sources and enjoy up to four views simultaneously on one massive screen. Viewers can keep the main event front and center while following other matchups and key moments at the same time, turning the screen into a complete game-day hub.
Behind all of these experiences is AWOL's flagship imaging platform. LuxVision features an RGB triple-laser light source covering 110% of Rec 2020, along with a 10,000:1 native contrast ratio with IRIS, seven-level Dynamic IRIS and Enhanced Black Level (EBL) technology. It also supports Dolby Vision, HDR10+ and IMAX Enhanced. Anti-RBE Technology II is designed to reduce rainbow artifacts during both 2D and 3D viewing.
Price and Availability
LuxVision is available for reservation from September 14 through November 2 on AWOL's official website. Customers who place a $100, €100, or £100 deposit can lock in the LuxVision Cinema System Launch Offer, which includes the LuxVision Cinema System and one of two eligible screen options: a 100"-150" New Gen Fresnel ALR Screen ($999-$4,999) or a 100"-120" New Gen Floor-Rising ALR Screen ($1,999-$2,999). 
LuxVision will officially launch on November 3, with an MSRP of $5,999 / €5,999 / £4,999. 
LuxVision is offered in three standard finishes: Eclipse Platinum, Boreal Oak, and Champagne Walnut. Customers may also choose a Custom CMF (Color, Material, and Finish) option for an additional $1,000 or add 4-channel HDMI Multiview for an additional $500.

articles.title: HyperX Cloud Alpha Air Review: Open-back and budget-friendly
articles.text:
Tom's Hardware Verdict
The Cloud Alpha Air is light, comfortable, and it sounds very good. It doesn't seem to work with HyperX's Ngenuity software, but you shouldn't need that to use this headset.
Reasons to buy
- + Very comfortable and lightweight
- + Sturdy
- + Sounds good
Reasons to avoid
- - Loud blip when you press the mute button
- - Extension system of wires is not ideal
- - Ngenuity doesn't work, at least not yet.
Why you can trust Tom's Hardware
Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.
HyperX has decided to toss its hat in the ring of open-back gaming headsets with its newest, the Cloud Alpha Air. It's definitely not the first open-back headset we've seen in the past few years — others include the $200 Corsair Virtuoso Pro, the $180 Turtle Beach Atlas Air, and, of course, the $900 Audeze LCD-GX. The Cloud Alpha Air is at least somewhat budget-friendly at just $149.99.
The Cloud Alpha Air is a wired over-ear open-back gaming headset designed for comfort and immersion. It features dynamic 40mm drivers with a frequency response range of 20 - 20,000 Hz and a special "HyperX Bass Tube" to keep the low end present without compromising the open-back design. And, like other HyperX headsets (which are some of the best gaming headsets we've tested), it's extremely lightweight and easy to wear for hours at a time.
Design and Comfort of the Cloud Alpha Air
The Cloud Alpha Air is a wired over-ear (circumaural) open-back headset with a detachable boom microphone. It has large, plastic oval-shaped earcups with metal grilles attached to a padded steel headband. It's a fairly lightweight headset — HyperX has its weight listed at 9.6 ounces (272g) without the boom mic attached (the boom mic is listed at approximately 0.42 ounces / 12g), but we found the headset weighed closer to 10 ounces (283g) (the boom mic, however, weighed closer to 0.07oz / 2g), and came in at just under 10.6 ounces (300g) with both the boom mic and cables attached. This still makes it one of HyperX's lightest headsets — slightly lighter than the HyperX Cloud Stinger 3 Wireless and Turtle Beach's Atlas Air open-back headset.
The Cloud Alpha Air's earcups are pretty roomy, with thick memory foam padding covered in soft ultrasuede material. The earcups tilt and swivel a little, but they're not as flexible as the earcups on many gaming headsets — and they don't swivel flat. The headset features a steel headband with leatherette-covered padding at the top and metal-reinforced yokes, so that explains the rigidity. The earcups are independently height-adjustable, with about an inch of extension for a maximum inner headband measurement of approximately 12 inches (300mm).
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
I found the Cloud Alpha Air to be very comfortable, despite the headband's relative rigidity, since the whole package is pretty lightweight and well-padded. However, I can see users with larger heads having problems with the top of the headband, as the padding did press on my crown slightly.
This is a wired headset, so there aren't a lot of ports or on-ear controls. The left earcup has two 3.5mm jacks, one for the detachable boom mic and one for the primary audio cable, as well as a microphone mute button, and the right earcup has a volume wheel.
The Cloud Alpha Air is wired, but the wires are detachable, and it comes with everything you need in the box to plug it into various devices. The main cable is a standard 4-foot (1.2m) 3.5mm, and it comes with two extension cables: a 4.5-foot (1.37m) 3.5mm to USB-C extension (with a USB-C to USB-A converter attached) for plugging it into a PC or console, and a 3.5-foot (1m) PC extension cable with separate audio and microphone jacks. That gets you about 8 - 8.5 feet of cable when you're plugged into your PC, which is decent — though I would personally prefer single long cables instead of the extension system, as the extension system means there's a weight (where the cables connect) in the middle. The cables are braided and seem high-quality, if a bit heavy. The headset also comes with its detachable boom microphone in the box, as well as a thick drawstring carrying bag for keeping everything together.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Specs
| Driver Type | 40mm dynamic | 
| Frequency Response | 20 - 20,000 Hz | 
| Design Style | Over-ear (circumaural), open-back | 
| Microphone Type | 10mm, uni-directional | 
| Connectivity | Wired (USB-C/A, 3.5mm) | 
| Weight | 10oz / 283g | 
| Cord Length | 4ft (3.5mm AUX) 4.5ft (3.5mm to USB-C) 3.5ft (3.5mm to | 
| Battery Life | N/A | 
| Lighting | None | 
| Software | HyperX Ngenuity | 
| MSRP / Price at Time of Review | $149.99 | 
| Release Date | Sept. 2026 | 
Audio Performance of the Cloud Alpha Air
The Cloud Alpha Air features dynamic 40mm neodymium drivers, with a frequency response range of 20 - 20,000 Hz (still pretty standard for gaming headsets, despite several companies coming out with premium models that have wider ranges).
Music sounds very good on the Cloud Alpha Air. The headset has a mostly neutral sound profile, with bright, detailed highs, a full, present mid-range, and solid but not overly powerful bass. It definitely has a wider sound stage than its closed-back counterparts, though it's not quite as wide or as open as some open-back headsets (such as the Audeze LCD-GX). Mid-range-heavy songs such as K-931's Lonely World and Enya's Orinoco Flow sounded especially dynamic. The headset has a built-in "HyperX Bass Tube" designed to maintain powerful bass, despite its open-back style. This works decently well — while I still found bass to be more powerful on closed-back headsets such as the Razer BlackShark V3 Pro, the bass was definitely present (and fairly detailed — I could hear the full run of the bass drum in Lorde's Royals).
Games sound even better on the Cloud Alpha Air, thanks to the open-back design. Games with multi-layered audio environments, such as Uncharted 4 and God of War: Ragnarok, really stood out on the headset — I could hear every individual creature in jungles and make out conversations with (possibly unrealistic) clarity in cities. Directional audio was also very good, though I would probably still opt for a closed-back headset for competitive first-person shooters where the direction of footsteps and gunshots is paramount. But you can't beat open-back headsets for exploring an open world (and for being able to hear things happening in the real world).
Microphone of the Cloud Alpha Air
The Cloud Alpha Air has a detachable 10mm boom microphone with a unidirectional polar pattern. It sits at the end of a 3-inch flexible metal gooseneck you can bend toward your mouth for better pickup, and the arm has a small red indicator light near the microphone end that lets you know when it's muted. It's the same microphone found on HyperX's other premium headsets, including the Cloud III S Wireless and the Cloud Alpha 2 Wireless.
The mic performs about as well as expected — it's good for a headset mic, but it's definitely still a headset mic. My voice was clear and full-sounding over both voice chat and in recordings. But the mic's pickup was pretty low by default — for other HyperX headsets I've been able to adjust the gain in its Ngenuity software, but I wasn't able to get Ngenuity to recognize the Cloud Alpha Air (I imagine if it had recognized it, it would have been adjustable, however). Hopefully this is fixed in a software or firmware update soon.
The mic mute button is easy to press, and the indicator light is a nice thought — but it was too low and too dim to be useful to me (I had to keep moving the mic up to see it, which seems like it sort of defeats the purpose of having an unobtrusive indicator light). I also had the same issue I did with the mute mic button on the HyperX Cloud III wired headset, where pressing the mute button caused a noticeable blip in my recordings.
Features and Software of the Cloud Alpha Air
The Cloud Alpha Air is supposed to be configurable with HyperX's Ngenuity peripheral software, which should let you do things such as tune the EQ and adjust the microphone's input gain. But, again, I couldn't get any version of Ngenuity to recognize the Cloud Alpha Air.
Bottom Line
If you've been thinking of getting an open-back gaming headset, the Cloud Alpha Air might be the headset you've been waiting for. As long as you don't mind the wires, it's an excellent headset for the price — it's comfortable, lightweight, and it sounds great whether you're listening to music, watching movies, or gaming. While I couldn't get it to connect to Ngenuity, I honestly don't count that as much of a point against it — peripheral software often causes more headaches than it's worth, especially for a headset that's mostly analog to begin with.
Sarah Jacobsson Purewal is a senior editor at Tom's Hardware covering peripherals, software, and custom builds. You can find more of her work in PCWorld, Macworld, TechHive, CNET, Gizmodo, Tom's Guide, PC Gamer, Men's Health, Men's Fitness, SHAPE, Cosmopolitan, and just about everywhere else.

articles.title: This 4K bird feeder camera nails focus, but its video frame rates let it down
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 Pro is a well-built, easy-to-live-with smart feeder that keeps itself charged and produces nicely detailed 4K footage of back yard birds. But a 15fps cap on 4K video, an ultra slow-motion mode that doesn’t appear to work properly, a cluttered app and AI-assisted species ID locked behind a subscription mean it falls slightly short of justifying its premium price.
Reasons to buy
- + Detailed 4K images with the right settings
- + Sturdy, rattle-free build and easy installation
- + Easily removable dual-chamber hopper
- + Solar roof keeps the battery topped up
Reasons to avoid
- - -Best software features require a subscription
- - 4K video capped at 15fps; 120fps mode doesn’t play back smoothly
- - Birds sometimes come closer than the minimum focus distance
- - Cluttered, confusing app
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 Pro: two-minute review
Smart bird feeders have quietly become one of the busiest corners of the camera world. Hang one in your yard, garden or on a balcony railing and it’ll snap and film every feathered visitor automatically, often identifing the species for you, too. We’ve tested plenty of them here at TechRadar — you’ll find the best in our guide to the best bird feeder cameras — and the Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 Pro is the latest to land in my garden.
If it looks familiar, that’s because it’s clearly a descendant of the Kiwibit Beako, which we tested last year. The headline upgrade is in the camera: Kiwibit says this is the first bird feeder camera to combine 4K HDR with phase-detection autofocus (PDAF), the kind of focusing tech you’ll find in a decent smartphone. The other big change is a roof with solar panels built into it, so there’s no separate panel to mount and wire up.
That roof turns out to be one of the feeder’s best features. After an initial charge I never needed to plug it in again during testing, and the battery hovered near full. The rest of the hardware impresses too: the plastic shell is tough and well finished, mounting it took minutes, and lifting out the two-chamber seed hopper for a refill or clean is about as easy as it gets.
The camera is a game of two halves, though. Photos and 4K clips are crisp, and the autofocus generally locks on to birds reliably — though ones that hop right into the seed tray can get too close for it focus. The biggest frustration is motion: 4K is limited to 15 frames per second, which makes footage look juddery, and the 120fps slow-motion mode currently produces clips that are little better than slideshows. The 1080p 60fps mode is the pick of the bunch.
Then there’s the app, which is cluttered and hard to navigate, and keeps its most compelling feature — AI species identification — behind a Kiwibit Plus subscription. That ID system was accurate in my testing, even if it can only name one species per clip. Taken as a whole, the Bird Feeder 2 Pro’s hardware is impressive, but its software and video modes need to catch up.
Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 Pro: price and availability
- $279.99 in the US with 'lifetime AI' included, or $219.99 without
- £289.99 in the UK; launching Q1 2027
- Kiwibit Plus subscription priced from $7.99 per month
The Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 Pro is currently on sale in the US for $219.99, or $279.99 with a lifetime subscription to the Kiwibit Plus service. It’s due to arrive in the UK in the first quarter of 2027, priced at £289.99.
That price puts it in premium territory, alongside the likes of the Bird Buddy 2. And there’s a running cost to factor in, because AI species identification and several other app features require a Kiwibit Plus subscription, which costs from $89.99 (a UK price is TBC) per year or $7.99 a month.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 Pro: key specs
| Camouflage EZ BirdFeed specs |  | 
|---|---|
| Photo | Up to 12MP | 
| Video | 4K at 15fps; 1080p at 60fps or 120fps | 
| Lens | 130-degree field of view | 
| Memory | Up to 128GB microSD card (not included) | 
| Dimensions | 9.8 x 8.7 x 8.9 inches / 25 x 22 x 22.7cm | 
| Weight | 4.08lbs / 1.85kg | 
| Connectivity | USB-C, Dual-band Wi-Fi 6 | 
| Battery | 5,200mAh battery, 5W solar panel | 
Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 Pro: design
- Solar panels built into the hinged roof
- Removable 1.7l dual-compartment hopper
- IP65 rated and works in -4F to 122F (-20C to 50C) temperature range
Side by side with the Kiwibit Beako, the Bird Feeder 2 Pro is almost a dead ringer. The one key difference is up on top, with the solar panels now built into the roof. It’s a smart move that cuts down on clutter, as you don’t need to find somewhere else to mount a panel or route a cable.
The same roof also hides one of the feeder’s best design touches. Flip it up (it just requires you to press a button to release a latch) and you can lift the seed hopper straight out to clean or refill it. That hopper has two compartments, so you can offer two different seed mixes if you like, and each one has its own sliding door for shutting off the supply.
The body is almost entirely plastic, which won’t appeal to everyone. There are wooden and metal bird feeder cameras out there, and personally I’d prefer either material on something that lives in my garden. I also wonder whether the green plastic will fade in the sun over time, although I didn’t notice any change in my few weeks of testing.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
On the plus side, this is solid, hard-wearing plastic, and the feeder feels sturdier than others I’ve reviewed — the hinged roof, for instance, opens and closes without a hint of rattle. It’s IP65 rated and Kiwibit says it’ll work in temperatures from -4F to 122F (-20C to 50C), so bad weather shouldn’t be a worry for the electronics inside.
My review sample came with three mounting options: a fabric strap for wrapping around a tree or lamppost, a pole mount for stick it on the top of poles up to one inch (25.4mm) in diameter, and a wall bracket. I used the bracket to fix the feeder to a trellis against the back wall of my courtyard garden, and it took no time at all. A positioning sticker in the box shows you where to drill two guide holes, then two screws (also supplied) hold the bracket in place. There are wall plugs in the box too, should you need them.
The feeder itself attaches to the bracket with four small hex screws, and the same screws secure the perch. An Allen key is included in the box, but make sure you keep it somewhere safe or have a spare, as you’ll be in a pickle without one. My sample also came with a water beaker that clips on to the perch.
Power comes from a rechargeable, removable battery that’s topped up by the solar roof panels, and the combination works very well. I fully charged the battery via USB-C before installation, as the manual instructs, and haven’t charged it manually since — weeks later, it’s still sitting at 99% capacity. To be fair, my testing took place in a sunny late summer and early autumn, and I positioned the feeder to catch a few hours of direct sun each day. I’m curious to see how it copes with the gloomier winter months here in southeast England.
Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 Pro: performance
- 4K video capped at 15fps
- AI species ID requires a Kiwibit Plus subscription
- Phase-detection autofocus with a 130-degree view
Some bird feeder cameras I’ve tested have struggled to stay connected to my home Wi-Fi, but the Bird Feeder 2 Pro’s dual-band connection was stable throughout, even though the signal was rarely at full strength. The live feed kicked in from my phone without much delay, whenever I requested it.
Everything runs through Kiwibit’s app, and frankly it isn’t very well designed. There are too many sections with vague names, I regularly forgot where things lived, and getting to my photos and videos took more taps than it should. A simpler, pared-back layout would make a big difference.
There are some nice touches, mind you. Each species gets a written description, the Nature Expert section answers your bird questions, and the Collection page gives you a quick rundown of every species your camera has spotted. The catch is that many of the best features — especially the AI species identification, which feels like a core reason to buy this feeder — sit behind a Kiwibit Plus subscription. Kiwibit gave me a code for a year’s access, but for everyone else it’s an extra $89.99 on top of an already premium price, and the feeder feels noticeably less capable without it.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
The identification itself was largely accurate. Only five species visited during my testing period, and the feeder correctly named four of them. That one miss was interesting, though: in a clip featuring a robin, a sparrow and a blue tit, only the robin was identified. That was the only clip containing a blue tit, so it appears the system tags just the first species it spots in each video. I’ve no doubt it would have recognized the blue tit on its own, but it’s a shame it can’t log multiple species in one clip.
Image quality is a more complicated story. 4K videos and photos generally look good, with plenty of sharpness and clarity, and the autofocus is accurate. There's even a microphone to capture sound, and it's nice to hear the birds chomping away on seeds or tweeting at each other. But 4K video is capped at just 15fps, which I found baffling. It makes clips look jerky, and it put me off using the 4K mode altogether. Why couldn't it just be 24fps or 30fps?
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
Shooting in 4K does have one perk: the software may automatically pull a 12MP Ultra HD “Keyshot” still from your footage. These are sharpened and upscaled for extra detail, but I found them a little over-sharpened, and they’re oddly large files at around 10MB each, given the modest resolution. You can’t pick the frame yourself, either — the software chooses for you, and it doesn’t always choose well. There’s a second type of auto photo, called SwiftShot, which is generated in Ultra Slow Motion mode and is meant to freeze birds in flight. That never happened for me; every SwiftShot I got showed a bird sitting on the feeder, and in noticeable less detail than with the Ultra HD Keyshots.
Video clips are 10 seconds long by default, but extendable to three minutes. I’d have liked to catch birds flying in more often, but my videos generally started with the visitor already perched.
There are two slow-motion modes, both 1080p: 60fps and 120fps. The 120fps mode doesn’t appear to work properly at the time of writing. Whatever settings I tried, the footage seemed to be captured at 15fps, so it plays back like a slideshow when slowed down. I was expecting something akin to the iPhone's buttery-smooth slow-motion mode, but this is in the single digits frames-per-second wise. I’ve reported this to Kiwibit and I hope a firmware update fixes it, because for now it’s useless as a video mode. It may be intended mainly for grabbing crisp stills of birds in motion, but since you can’t choose the frame yourself and have to rely on Kiwibit’s cloud processing to pick it, that’s not much consolation.
The 60fps mode is far better. Played back at half speed you get smooth 30fps slow motion, or at quarter speed you get the same 15fps as the 4K clips. It lacks the fine detail of 4K, but its smoothness at normal and half speed makes it the sweet spot of the lineup for me. One quirk to note: neither slow-motion mode records sound, even when you play clips back at normal speed.
Autofocus is generally reliable, but birds that came right into the seed tray, rather than staying on the perch, were sometimes out of focus. They seem to be inside the minimum focus distance, which was also an issue with the Beako. It’s not a huge deal, but it’s annoying when a bird’s body is sharp and its eyes and beak are soft.
Sharing and saving photos and videos is easy – you just hit the share button when viewing in the app and you get the option to download the file to your phone, or share via a variety of means. Subscribers also get cloud storage for all their files.
Should you buy the Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 Pro?
Buy it if...
You want detailed 4K stills
Its 4K photos are sharp and clear, and the phase-detection autofocus is accurate.
You never want to charge a battery
The solar roof kept the battery near full for weeks without me plugging it in once.
You want easy upkeep
The removable two-chamber hopper makes refilling and cleaning quick and lets you offer two seed mixes.
Don't buy it if...
You want smooth video
4K is capped at 15fps, and the 120fps slow-motion mode currently plays back like a slideshow.
You don’t want a subscription
AI species identification, a key selling point, is locked behind Kiwibit Plus.
You’d prefer a natural-looking feeder
It’s almost entirely plastic, so look elsewhere if you’d rather have wood or metal in your garden.
Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 Pro: also consider
Bird Buddy 2
Priced at around $299 / £300, the Bird Buddy 2 also has a solar roof, and its app is far more polished and enjoyable to use, with free AI species ID. Its standard video is only at 1080p resolution, though, with 2K reserved for subscribers.
Read our Bird Buddy 2 review
Camouflage EZ BirdFeed
If you’re in Europe and value matters more than image quality, this £139 feeder is hard to beat. It offers AI bird ID with no subscription and twin roof-mounted solar panels, but its 1080p images can’t match the Kiwibit’s crisp detail.
Read our Camouflage EZ BirdFeed review
How I tested the Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 Pro
- Mounted on a garden trellis for several weeks in late summer/early fall
- Tested all video modes, including both slow-motion settings
- Used the app with a Kiwibit Plus subscription
I installed the Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 Pro in my garden in southeast England using the supplied wall bracket, fixing it to a trellis in a spot that got a few hours of direct sunlight a day. After fully charging the battery via USB, I left it to run on solar power for the rest of the testing period, which ran through late summer into early autumn.
I tested the feeder with the Kiwibit app on my phone, using a year’s Kiwibit Plus subscription supplied by Kiwibit to access the AI species ID and other premium features. I tried every video mode, including 4K and both 1080p slow-motion settings, compared the automatically generated KeyShot and SwiftShot stills, and checked the AI identifications against the birds I could see in each clip.
- First reviewed October 2026
Sam has been writing about tech and digital culture for over 20 years, starting off in video games journalism before branching out into the wonderful worlds of consumer electronics, streaming entertainment and photography. Over the years he has written for Wired, Stuff, GQ, T3, Trusted Reviews and PC Zone, and now lives on the Kent coast in the UK – the ideal place for a camera reviewer to ply their trade.

articles.title: Cancellation: A creator’s biggest turning point; Scaling India’s research multiplier
articles.text:
Cancellation: A creator’s biggest turning point; Scaling India’s research multiplier
At TechSparks 2026, Varun Mayya, Founder and CEO of AEOS, a content and media-tech company, spoke about how online backlash can free creators to speak their minds, why founders need to get comfortable with reinvention, and why there is no secret formula for going viral.
Dear Reader,
Food safety has come under intense scrutiny in recent times.
The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India has now proposed a ban on adding sucrose and fructose to food products for infants up to the age of six months. The measure aims to reduce infants’ exposure to added sugars and tackle health risks linked to childhood obesity.
In other related news, Maharashtra’s Food and Drug Administration has named officials of Reliance Group entities and Eternal’s Blinkit and Hyperpure units, including Blinkit CEO Albinder Dhindsa, in a probe over expired food products. The products have allegedly re-entered the food supply chain, according to case documents reviewed by Reuters.
Meanwhile, amid rising concerns of AI safety, Anthropic has pitched its own safety bill to Capitol Hill lawmakers.
According to the proposal, the government could block release or deter deployment of an AI model if it poses an imminent risk of causing more than $1 billion in damages or killing or seriously injuring more than 50 people, Politico reported, citing three people.
Moving on, French carmaker Renault is betting big on hybrid and CNG technology in India.
Renault India CEO Stephane Deblaise believes both technologies could account for almost half of the automaker’s powertrain sales mix over the next 2-3 years. On Saturday, the automaker launched its first strong hybrid offering on the Duster SUV; it plans to launch factory-fitted CNG models in the future.
In today’s newsletter, we will talk about
- Cancellation: A creator’s biggest turning point
- Scaling India’s research multiplier
Here’s your trivia for today: In which country was the world’s first ATM installed? (Scroll down for the answer)
Content creation
Cancellation: A creator’s biggest turning point
At TechSparks 2026, Varun Mayya, Founder and CEO of AEOS, a content and media-tech company, spoke about how online backlash can free creators to speak their minds, why founders need to get comfortable with reinvention, and why there is no secret formula for going viral.
Finding an audience takes more than posting regularly on social media. It requires years of experimentation, a willingness to stand apart, and the ability to adapt as technology and audience expectations change, according to the content creator and entrepreneur.
Key takeaways:
- For Mayya, brand building comes down to two things. The first is simply having the courage to put yourself out there. The second is differentiation. When young founders stand out, they can even raise funding at a time when they have few other markers of success.
- Speaking on cancellation and criticism, Mayya said, “Once you've been cancelled, then you can say whatever you want. And I think that has been really valuable. As long as you understand that not everyone’s going to be on your side, then you’re okay.”
- When it comes to viral content, Mayya doesn’t believe there’s a secret formula to crack. He argued that recommendation algorithms largely reflect what people want to watch. Creators need to understand and mirror what their audience cares about.
R&D
Scaling India’s research multiplier
India cannot afford to replicate the 75-year evolutionary timelines of Western institutions like the US National Science Foundation or DARPA, according to Shivkumar Kalyanaraman, Chief Executive Officer of the Anusandhan National Research Foundation.
To boost India’s R&D spend toward 3% of GDP, Kalyanaraman reveals a patient-capital architecture combining private investment, open IP licensing, and national mission programmes.
Key takeaways
- Speaking at TechSparks 2026, YourStory’s annual summit, Kalyanaraman outlined how the nation is altering its approach to scientific research and technology commercialisation.
- Formalised by Parliament in 2023 following recommendations in the National Education Policy 2020, the Anusandhan National Research Foundation operates as an autonomous statutory body presided over by the Prime Minister of India. The organisation, he said, must bypass traditional bureaucratic friction and drive scientific discovery into the real economy at unprecedented speed.
- At the centre of transformation is the Research, Development, and Innovation fund, a government-backed pool of Rs 1 lakh crore. Designed as a patient capital instrument, the fund provides long-term financial support tailored to research-intensive and deeptech enterprises that require extended gestation periods without demanding immediate short-term returns.
News & updates
- ICICI Bank: ICICI Bank has reported a higher-than-expected profit for its second quarter, driven by stronger loan demand and lower provisions for bad loans. The country’s second-largest private lender by market capitalisation posted a standalone net profit of Rs 148.43 billion for the three months ended September, compared with Rs 123.59 billion a year earlier.
- HDFC Bank: HDFC Bank reported a second-quarter profit that narrowly missed analyst expectations, as weaker treasury income and higher provisions for bad loans offset strong lending growth. The lender also said in a regulatory filing that its deputy managing director Kaizad Bharucha will step down at the end of December.
- ixigo Q2: Travel and ticket booking platform ixigo has reported a consolidated net profit of Rs 63.42 crore for the September quarter, aided by the partial sale of stake in Freshbus, an intercity electric bus operator and smart mobility startup, and strong growth in the hotel bookings segment. Hotels emerged as ixigo’s fastest-growing business line by gross transaction value.
In which country was the world’s first ATM installed?
Answer: The United Kingdom

articles.title: Science says your boss should talk less in meetings
articles.text:
Close to 1 billion meetings take place each day around the world. CEOs spend nearly three-quarters of their workdays in meetings. Planning for and spearheading meetings eats up the lion’s share of managers’ time. In much of the industrialized world, meetings are both the metronomes and menaces of people’s working lives.
Given the enormous time spent in workplace meetings, do we know what they accomplish or how to make them as worthwhile as possible? For decades, the answer was… not really. Meetings weren’t a particularly accessible subject of study. But that has changed. Once a tiny niche area, “meeting science” is a growing specialization among organizational and social psychologists. The field is accelerating as archived virtual meetings provide vast swaths of data. And it is providing a fascinating window into human behavior.
Meeting to talk helps fulfill basic human needs to connect, communicate, and cooperate. People have long come together—in caves, fields, market squares, and town halls—to get something done, share ideas, get on the same page, or just to remark on the weather. But meeting scientists define their subject as gatherings of people “with some goal or structure to the event,” says organizational psychologist Liana Kreamer of the Florida Institute of Technology, who coauthored a review of over three decades of meeting science in the 2026 Annual Review of Organizational Psychology and Organizational Behavior.
As a graduate student, Kreamer was interested in studying teamwork, leadership, and work relationships. During her doctorate work with meeting scientist Steven Rogelberg, she realized that meetings would be a fine venue for studying all of that and more. “You can use a meeting as a stage to study anything you want,” she says. After all, at their core “meetings are a fundamental aspect of how we organize and interact as social beings,” Kreamer and coauthors Rogelberg and Jon Gray, both of the University of North Carolina in Charlotte, wrote in the 2026 article.
To tap meetings for study, researchers typically use two approaches. The first is a classic survey in which researchers retroactively ask people about their real or simulated meeting experiences and analyze the responses. The second method is to analyze specific behaviors and trends extracted from audio and video recordings of meetings. Such precise content is “where the music is,” says industrial and organizational psychologist Nale Lehmann-Willenbrock, director of the Center for Better Work at the University of Hamburg, Germany.
In one experiment, Lehmann-Willenbrock and colleagues extracted data from video-recorded meetings to study how leader communication affects team interaction during decision-making. The researchers found that respectful, attentive inquiry by meeting leaders enhanced team performance, in contrast to when leaders asked questions but didn’t attentively listen to responses.
Leading with listening
As with many meeting science studies, their findings about what improves meetings’ effectiveness often seem obvious, but meeting researchers note that meetings often stray far from these ideals.
Such research also consistently reveals the importance of active listening, says Lehmann-Willenbrock: not just passive acknowledgement by the listener but actively providing thoughtful feedback. In virtual meetings, because “we’ve all learned to mute ourselves if we’re not talking, very often, active listening is killed completely.”
The balance of listening and speaking also can influence how well a meeting goes. Meeting leaders and participants may retain very different views of whether a meeting was successful, notes Lehmann-Willenbrock. “Often, leaders talk the most, which is also why they often think their meetings are pretty good,” she says. Kreamer also emphasizes that it’s important that meeting leaders lead but not dominate the discussion. Leaders should monitor the proportion of time they are speaking to allow for inclusion of many voices.
Research supports a checklist of additional things that leaders can do before, during, and after a meeting to make it a success, says Lehmann-Willenbrock. To set the stage, leaders should choose appropriate rooms, refreshments, and lighting, invite only those who need to be there, plan to start and end on time, prepare an agenda, set and communicate clear goals, and allow time for pre-meeting conversation.
Socializing first, especially in virtual meetings, is beneficial, Lehmann-Willenbrock says. Her research has shown that “for more introverted participants and more quiet participants, this warmup phase is really helpful because it helps them make more active contributions inside the meeting.”
Indeed, her studies on face-to-face meetings have shown that pre-meeting small talk predicts meeting effectiveness, particularly for more introverted participants. But pre-meeting talk is rare in virtual meetings; she says leaders should consider establishing a norm of arriving early or using the first few minutes for an informal check-in.
Engaging attendees
Facilitators can increase the likelihood of a successful meeting by making sure all opinions are heard. Kreamer recommends a technique called silent brainstorming to get all participants, even shy and reluctant ones, to engage in idea generation. It involves creating a shared virtual space, such as a chat or online document, to which all participants contribute simultaneously. Kreamer points to a 2009 study that found this approach (some researchers call it “brainwriting”) was more effective than traditional free-for-all spoken brainstorming in meetings.
Kreamer uses this technique when she and her students are dreaming up research ideas in class. “We can all see each other working,” she says, and the quieter students don’t worry about interrupting or having to verbally express their suggestions. After 10 minutes, she reviews the ideas with the group.
Zofia Walters, a doctoral student in industrial organizational psychology working with Kreamer, has been studying another aspect of meeting inclusiveness: the needs of neurodiverse participants. Her studies provide evidence that while practices like minimizing distractions, documenting instructions, using shared calendars, and building regular check-ins into meetings likely benefit all employees, they may be especially helpful for people with ADHD.
In a survey of 147 employees from a variety of workplaces, Walters asked participants about their most recent virtual meeting: how effective it was, how fatigued they felt afterward and their emotional state. Participants also reported how much time they spent multitasking during the meeting, such as by answering emails, and how long their camera was on. They also shared whether they had an ADHD diagnosis, either formal or informal (based on self-assessment).
In findings yet to be published, Walters reported that individuals with ADHD were more likely to report feeling more meeting fatigue, especially when the camera was on for extended periods, than non-ADHD peers. They also reported poorer emotional states. Her findings also suggest that multitasking during meetings may help ADHD attendees manage boredom or hyperactivity.
Effective meeting practices don’t end when the meeting ends. After a meeting, leaders can ensure it was time well spent by communicating action items to participants, taking concrete steps to implement the ideas and tasks generated in the meeting, and assessing employee engagement, meeting satisfaction, and meeting effectiveness, Lehmann-Willenbrock and colleagues concluded in a 2018 paper in Organizational Dynamics.
The downsides—and upsides
Does all this time spent in meetings take a toll on workers? The evidence seems to suggest so. Research has found that employees anticipate feeling worse and being less productive when their day is jam-packed with meetings, especially when they are working on complex tasks.
Meetings are sometimes seen as the default way to get things done, but often, people don’t specify what they want to achieve from them, says cognitive scientist Ava Scott of the University of Copenhagen. This, she says, “makes a lot of meetings feel very purposeless.”
Recurring meetings tend to be the most aimless, Scott’s research on Microsoft employees has found; one participant described the content of these successive meets as dreamlike in their similarity to one another. If there’s no clear goal, you don’t know why you’re meeting, and everyone’s very busy, it probably indicates that taking up people’s time with a meeting isn’t ideal, says Scott. Kreamer notes that some companies, such as Shopify, have cut all recurring meetings.
Nevertheless, a 2026 study of more than 9,000 workers in Norway found that while meetings are both common and costly, their benefits may make them worth enduring. The research, led by economist David Deming at Harvard University and based on data collected by Norwegian survey company Norstat, found that meeting intensity is positively associated with subsequent wage growth and on-the-job learning. One possible explanation for the finding is that these meetings may offer the chance to interact with more senior colleagues and so enable the transmission of key knowledge.
The important caveat is that the study, published by the National Bureau of Economic Research, was correlational, so it can’t establish a causal relationship between the number of meetings attended and wage increases; it does further suggest that although the cost of meetings is particularly high for high-wage companies, the benefits may be even higher. That leads the authors to conclude: “Meetings are the broccoli of work—widely disliked, but probably good for us anyway.”
Strategies for success
Humor can help make a meeting successful—as long as it’s authentic, supportive, or positive rather than demeaning. Used appropriately, humor can spur new ideas and enhance team performance. This is most likely to work when meeting participants are well-acquainted, Lehmann-Willenbrock reported after analyzing videos of meetings at two German companies. People have to know each other well enough to feel safe making a joke, she says.
But not everyone is comfortable using humor in meetings, says science educator and comedian Vita Stout, now at Sierra College in Rocklin, California. The former bat researcher attended the International Congress for Bat Research in Austin, Texas, in 2022, and took notes on the jokes being used in meeting talks—transcribing exact quotes, their timing, and audience response. Stout’s research, coauthored with bat scientists and published in the Proceedings of Biological Sciences B, argued that when well-timed and used appropriately, humor in scientific meetings can be a tool for connection and community-building. But joke-telling was more prominent among meeting participants with privilege and power, with older, well-established male scientists making jokes more frequently than early career researchers and scientists from underrepresented groups.
As in comedy, timing is also key when planning meetings. Scheduling should consider the human circadian rhythm and avoid meeting during the after-lunch energy dip. Lehmann-Willenbrock admits ruefully that her own academic environment often doesn’t obey that rule. “A lot of our committee meetings are scheduled when people are at their most tired,” she says, or digesting lunch.
It’s also important to be mindful of people’s work and family obligations in meeting scheduling. “I have two small kids,” she says, “and I always get really angry when a meeting gets called that’s about something… diversity- or inclusion-related, and then it’s scheduled at 5 pm.”
Some research suggests there are cultural differences in basic expectations for meetings. In a survey of 1,432 workers from six countries, for example, Lehmann-Willenbrock and collaborators measured how frustrated, irritated, and upset individuals became in imagined scenarios in which leaders or other participants showed up five, 10, or 15 minutes late to meetings. Respondents from the United States and the Netherlands were especially perturbed by a late leader and a high degree of lateness. People from China and Chile weren’t so frustrated by the same situations.
There are very few cross-cultural studies like this in the world of meeting science, says Kreamer. “We have these best practices of meetings that we’ve learned over the past 30 years,” she says, but the bulk of studies have come out of Europe or North America. That’s a deficit she’d like to see addressed to see whether the same rules for optimal meeting success apply. As soon as those results are out, we’ll have to call another meeting.

articles.title: Steam revoit son système de succès : voici ce qui va changer pour les joueurs
articles.text:
Terminer un jeu à 100 % peut devenir plus compliqué lorsqu’une extension ajoute de nouveaux défis après coup. Steam teste un système qui permet de mieux organiser les succès et de conserver les récompenses déjà obtenues, même lorsque le contenu d’un jeu évolue.
Le conflit entre DLC et complétion empoisonnait (on exagère à peine) l’expérience de nombreux joueurs Steam depuis des années. Lorsqu’un studio publiait du contenu additionnel après qu’un joueur avait décroché l’intégralité des succès d’un jeu, les nouveaux objectifs s’ajoutaient automatiquement à la liste commune, brisant fatalement son statut de complétion. Valve s’attaque enfin à ce problème avec les « Ensembles de succès », un nouveau système qui permet de mieux organiser les objectifs à débloquer.
Steam sépare les succès de vos jeux en plusieurs catégories
Dorénavant, chaque groupe possèdera sa propre barre de progression. Une fois tous les succès d’une série débloqués, un trophée de complétion apparaîtra sur le profil du joueur. Si de nouveaux succès rejoignent ultérieurement ce groupe, le trophée sera donc préservé.
Voici comment Steam présente sa nouvelle fonctionnalité : « Au fil du développement d’un jeu, les développeurs peuvent créer de nouvelles séries pour les contenus ajoutés. Ces nouvelles séries permettent aux joueurs réguliers de voir facilement ce qu’ils peuvent encore débloquer, tout en préservant leur statut de complétion antérieur ».
Concrètement, les studios pourront organiser les succès selon le type de contenu. Par exemple, un jeu pourra distinguer les défis du mode solo de ceux du multijoueur. Les joueurs qui ne pratiquent que la campagne pourraient ainsi terminer le groupe correspondant sans pour autant être pénalisés par des objectifs en ligne hors de leur portée. Pratique !
Des succès archivables et des séries temporaires
Steam donne également aux développeurs la possibilité d’archiver des succès individuels ou des séries entières, ouvrant ainsi la porte aux objectifs saisonniers et aux défis limités dans le temps. « Nous pensons qu’il existe de nombreuses façons amusantes d’exploiter ce caractère temporaire, comme ajouter des succès dans des jeux saisonniers ou activer des succès de fêtes éphémères », indique Valve.
Les succès archivés disparaissent du profil des joueurs qui les ont manqués sans bloquer leur progression vers la complétion d’une série. Valve cite le cas des serveurs multijoueurs fermés définitivement : si certains succès en ligne deviennent impossibles à obtenir, ils peuvent être archivés, rendant la complétion du contenu solo de nouveau accessible.
Parmi les dix-sept jeux participant à la bêta figurent notamment Portal 2, Left 4 Dead 2, Team Fortress 2, Forza Horizon 5, Crusader Kings III, Euro Truck Simulator 2, American Truck Simulator, LEGO Batman: Legacy of the Dark Knight ou encore Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4.
Source : VGC

articles.title: Les Japonais ne changent pas leur huile moteur comme les Français, et leurs voitures dépassent souvent les 300 000 km
articles.text:
Les Japonais ne changent pas leur huile moteur comme les Français, et leurs voitures dépassent souvent les 300 000 km
Les automobilistes japonais sont encouragés à remplacer bien plus souvent leur huile moteur et leurs voitures sont capables de dépasser les 300 000 kilomètres. Plus exactement, c’est tous les 5 000 kilomètres ou six mois que ce remplacement est souvent recommandé au Japon.
En France, c’est différent avec, pour certains modèles, entre 20 000 et 30 000 kilomètres entre deux passages à l’atelier. Toyota et Honda, marques japonaises, dominent les études sur les voitures capables de dépasser 300 000 kilomètres.
Les Japonais changent plus souvent l'huile du moteur
Les petits trajets, les bouchons et les démarrages répétés du moteur empêchent l’huile de chauffer assez longtemps. De l’humidité et de l’essence se mélangent alors plus facilement à l’huile alors que les additifs perdent leur efficacité naturellement au fil du temps. Une huile trop vieille protège donc bien moins les surfaces métalliques et favorise les dépôts qui accélèrent l’usure interne.
Les Japonais l’ont bien compris et un remplacement de l’huile tous les 5 000 kilomètres ou six mois est souvent recommandé. Chez Toyota, un moteur essence sans turbo peut monter à 15 000 kilomètres en conditions normales, mais tombe à 7 500 kilomètres lorsqu’elles sont sévères. Pour un moteur turbo, le seuil peut même descendre à 5 000 kilomètres ou six mois, voire 2 500 kilomètres ou trois mois.
Mais alors pourquoi les Japonais ont comme consigne des constructeurs de changer leur huile plus régulièrement que chez nous ? Là-bas, on trouve beaucoup de petits trajets, embouteillages ou encore une circulation lente avec des redémarrages répétés en zones urbaines. Il y a aussi le parc automobile japonais à prendre en compte puisque les petites voitures et les moteurs turbo sont très nombreux et demandent une vidange plus fréquente.
En France, il existe les mêmes conditions qu'au Japon, évidemment. Mais on trouve plus de trajets périurbains, ruraux et interurbains plus longs. Par exemple, en milieu rural, 62,1 % des actifs parcourent plus de 10 km pour aller travailler. Les distances domicile-travail atteignent en moyenne 12 à 18 km. Alors sur ces parcours plus longs, le moteur et l'huile sont davantage à la bonne température, ce qui limite l'accumulation d'humidité et de carburant.
Les modèles japonais atteignent facilement 300 000 km
En France, le remplacement de l’huile moteur est bien moins fréquent sur certains modèles. Un Renault Captur TCe 130 est généralement vidangé tous les 30 000, 60 000 ou 90 000 kilomètres. Pour certaines Peugeot 308, c’est 20 000 kilomètres ou un an. Un automobiliste français parcourt donc parfois quatre à six fois plus de kilomètres entre deux vidanges qu’un automobiliste japonais.
Les études de longévité montrent que les marques japonaises dominent sur le terrain de la longévité. Le mois dernier, une étude basée sur plus de 395 millions de véhicules a calculé la probabilité d’atteindre 402 000 kilomètres. La Toyota Sequoia atteint 42,3 %
Puis on trouve derrière la Toyota 4Runner et la Toyota Tacoma, respectivement à 33,1 % et 25 %. Pour la Honda Civic, c’est 15 %. Karl Brauer, analyste chez iSeeCars, explique : "Atteindre 402 000 kilomètres est encore loin d’être habituel.”
Justement, un Toyota Tacoma a dépassé le 1,7 million de kilomètres avec son moteur d’origine. C’est Sasa Bolesnikov, propriétaire d’un atelier qui a suivi ce véhicule sur plus d’un million de kilomètres. Il explique que l’équipe a fait "guère plus que des vidanges régulières tous les 8 000 kilomètres". Il faut également noter que ce modèle roulait en Arizona, une zone où la corrosion est plus limitée que dans des territoires comme le Japon.

articles.title: Los 10 juegos peor calificados de Steam, según las reseñas de sus usuarios
articles.text:
Las reseñas de Steam pueden ayudar a evaluar un juego antes de comprarlo, aunque las preferencias y expectativas varían entre usuarios. En esta lista, diez títulos tienen calificaciones inferiores a 2,5 sobre 10 y una recepción mayoritariamente negativa, según los datos disponibles.
Los motivos de las críticas cambian de un juego a otro: algunos recibieron cuestionamientos por su estado técnico o desarrollo, mientras que otros decepcionaron a seguidores de franquicias conocidas. A continuación, una lista de 10 videojuegos con peor valoración en Steam.
1. War of the Three Kingdoms — 1,03/10
Con una puntuación de apenas 1,03 sobre 10, War of the Three Kingdoms ocupa el primer lugar entre los juegos peor calificados de Steam en esta lista. No se trata de una valoración basada en unas pocas opiniones: el título acumula más de 81.000 reseñas, de las cuales solo el 10 % son positivas, según los datos proporcionados.
2. Command & Conquer 4: Tiberian Twilight — 1,66/10
La cuarta entrega de Command & Conquer obtuvo una calificación de 1,66 sobre 10 y apenas un 17 % de reseñas positivas. Una de las principales críticas fue que el juego se apartó de lo que parte de los seguidores esperaba de la saga. En una franquicia con una comunidad consolidada, los cambios de diseño pueden influir en la recepción.
3. Conqueror’s Blade: Three Kingdoms — 1,69/10
Conqueror’s Blade: Three Kingdoms registra una nota de 1,69 sobre 10. Solo el 16 % de las reseñas son positivas. Su puntuación sitúa al juego entre los peor recibidos de la plataforma, aunque el promedio por sí solo no explica qué aspectos específicos motivaron las críticas de los usuarios.
4. Spacebase DF-9 — 1,79/10
El juego de construcción y gestión espacial Spacebase DF-9 tiene una puntuación de 1,79 sobre 10 y un 18 % de reseñas positivas. Su desarrollo fue polémico y, de acuerdo con las críticas recogidas, el estado en que quedó el proyecto contribuyó a la decepción de muchos jugadores.
5. Uriel’s Chasm — 1,83/10
Con 1,83 sobre 10, Uriel’s Chasm aparece entre los títulos con menor puntuación de Steam. El 18 % de sus reseñas son positivas. Aunque no tiene la misma notoriedad que otras franquicias de la lista, su promedio muestra que la mayoría de quienes lo reseñaron tuvo una experiencia desfavorable.
6. FlatOut 3: Chaos & Destruction — 1,84/10
FlatOut 3: Chaos & Destruction obtuvo una puntuación de 1,84 sobre 10 y apenas un 18 % de reseñas positivas. Las críticas estuvieron relacionadas con la comparación frente a las entregas anteriores de la saga. Para muchos seguidores, el juego no alcanzó el nivel que esperaban de la serie.
7. MOBILE SUIT GUNDAM BATTLE OPERATION 2 — 2,21/10
La franquicia Gundam cuenta con numerosos seguidores, pero eso no evitó que MOBILE SUIT GUNDAM BATTLE OPERATION 2 recibiera una calificación baja en Steam. El título tiene 2,21 sobre 10 y un 22 % de reseñas positivas. Además, suma más de 21.000 opiniones, por lo que su promedio se basa en una cantidad considerable de comentarios.
8. STAR WARS: Battlefront Classic Collection — 2,43/10
La colección reúne juegos ligados a una de las sagas más reconocidas del entretenimiento, pero su recepción en Steam fue negativa. STAR WARS: Battlefront Classic Collection registra 2,43 sobre 10 y un 24 % de reseñas positivas. Entre los motivos señalados por los usuarios estuvieron los problemas técnicos que afectaron su lanzamiento.
9. Mirror 2: Project X — 2,44/10
Con más de 115.000 reseñas, Mirror 2: Project X destaca por el volumen de opiniones que ha recibido. Pese a esa cantidad, mantiene una calificación de 2,44 sobre 10 y solo un 24 % de reseñas positivas. La cifra refleja una recepción mayoritariamente desfavorable entre quienes publicaron una opinión en Steam.
10. THE 4 SINS — 2,45/10
THE 4 SINS cierra la lista con una puntuación de 2,45 sobre 10. Aunque es la más alta entre los diez juegos incluidos, sigue por debajo de 2,5 y cuenta con un 24 % de reseñas positivas. La baja calificación indica que la mayoría de los usuarios que lo reseñaron no lo recomienda.
Qué revisar antes de comprar un juego en Steam
Las puntuaciones pueden servir como primera referencia, pero no siempre explican por qué un título gustó o decepcionó. Antes de comprar, conviene revisar las reseñas recientes y buscar comentarios sobre aspectos concretos, como el rendimiento, los problemas técnicos, el contenido y las decisiones de diseño.
También es útil comprobar si las críticas se relacionan con preferencias personales o con fallas que podrían afectar la experiencia de juego. Así, las opiniones de otros usuarios ayudan a tomar una decisión con más contexto que el promedio por sí solo.

articles.title: China ha encontrado en la Luna una cápsula del tiempo de hierro, ahora solo queda aprender a abrirla
articles.text:
En la carrera por la colonización de la Luna, hay algo que China ha conseguido y que Estados Unidos aún no ha podido lograr: tomar muestras de su lado oculto. La encargada de hacerlo fue la misión Chang’e 6. Tras aterrizar en la cara oculta de nuestro satélite el 1 de junio de 2024, tomó casi 2 kg de muestras, que fueron devueltas a la Tierra unas semanas más tarde. Se han estado analizando desde entonces, pero uno de sus hallazgos más importantes se ha hecho esperar hasta ahora, pues en un estudio publicado recientemente se describe la presencia en las muestras de hierro gamma. Por supuesto que cabía esperar que hubiese hierro, pero no en esta conformación.
Hierro congelado en el tiempo. Cuando el hierro se encuentra por debajo de los 912ºC, se ordena siguiendo la conformación alfa, que es básicamente la que estamos acostumbrados a ver. Sin embargo, entre 912ºC y 1.394ºC puede tomar la conformación gamma, en la que los átomos siguen una estructura cúbica centrada en las caras. La temperatura de la Luna suele oscilar entre -248ºC y 121ºC. Por lo tanto, el hierro puro debería estar siempre en conformación alfa. Solo se convertiría en hierro gamma por un aumento gigantesco de temperatura, como el que se produciría con el impacto de un meteorito.
Posiblemente, después hubo un enfriamiento igual de súbito que dejó el hierro “congelado” en el estado en el que se encontraba. A esto se sumarían las pequeñas cantidades de carbono presentes en el meteorito, que ayudan a estabilizar aún más la estructura. Sería un proceso similar al del del temple del acero, cuando se enfría de golpe para conservar la forma que se le ha dado.
Hipótesis sobre magnetismo. Lo único que está realmente claro en esta historia es que el hierro gamma no debería existir en la Luna. La historia sobre cómo llegó a quedarse allí es solo una hipótesis de los autores del estudio que se ha publicado en PNAS. Esa hipótesis, además, sugiere que el hierro podría darnos información interesante sobre el pasado de la Luna. Y es que las partículas de hierro gamma más grandes que encontraron los investigadores formaron estructuras magnéticas estables y respondieron bien a campos magnéticos externos. Algunos materiales funcionan como una grabadora natural: cuando se enfrían, guardan una huella del campo magnético que había en ese momento.
La Luna no tiene campo magnético hoy en día, pero hay dudas sobre si lo tuvo en el pasado. Por eso, si en el momento que se “congeló” el hierro había un campo magnético en la Luna, podría darnos información sobre él.
Por qué es importante. Ya hemos visto que casi todo aquí son hipótesis. Aun así, es un hallazgo importante por muchos motivos. Para empezar, porque estamos ante un material único, ya que procede de una región de la Luna prácticamente inexplorada. Por otro lado, el hierro que se ha encontrado no debería existir a la temperatura lunar, por lo que está claro de que debe ser algo excepcional. Y por supuesto, también es un hallazgo importante por todo lo que podría contarnos sobre la Luna si las hipótesis que se han lanzado terminasen confirmándose.
¿Y ahora qué? Los autores de este estudio, procedentes de la Academia China de Ciencias, esperan conseguir más muestras con estos materiales, tanto de misiones ya devueltas como de futuras misiones de retorno de muestras lunares. Esto debería permitirles seguir escalando para confirmar o desmentir su hipótesis. Aún es pronto para ello, pero ya hemos visto todos los motivos por los que es una investigación muy especial. En realidad, las misiones Chang’e nos dieron muchas noticias especiales sobre la Luna.

En Xataka | La NASA necesita unas muestras lunares recogidas por China. Y para ello va a tener que saltarse la ley

articles.title: MapQuest adds a new Surveillance Layer so you know where all the Flock cameras are, and it's gone down well with users
articles.text:
'This is how you win back users': after a surge in popularity, MapQuest will now show you where Flock cameras are on the map
A new Surveillance Layer
- MapQuest is adding a new Surveillance Layer to its app
- It shows licence plate scanners from Flock and other companies
- The move seems to have gone down well online
MapQuest has been enjoying a resurgence in popularity since it decided to ignore certain lake renaming mandates from the US government, and a new feature freshly added to its Android and iOS apps may well improve its reputation further: Flock camera tracking.
According to the MapQuest announcement, (via Android Authority) the new Surveillance Layer in map options will bring up the locations of automated license plate readers (ALPRs) from the likes of Flock, Vigilant, Genetic, Axis, Axon, Leonardo, Neology, Rekor, PlateSmart, Ubicquia, and Verkada.
Considering that Flock alone has more than 120,000 cameras installed around the US, you're likely to see a worrying number of dots show up around you on the map when you switch this on — each represented by a searching red eye.
Such is the density of these ALPRs, you may not be able to completely avoid them without some very clever loops and shortcuts, but you will at least know they're there. You might decide it's better for your privacy to take the bus.
Use and misuse
The Roads Have Eyes! 👁️ Turn on the Surveillance Layer in Map Options to see known license plate readers from Flock Safety, Motorola Solutions (Vigilant), Genetec, Axis Communications, Axon, Leonardo (ELSAG), Neology, Rekor, PlateSmart, Ubicquia, Verkada, and other outdoor surveillance cameras.
— @mapquest.com (@mapquest.com.bsky.social) 2026-10-17T13:05:19.118Z
The arguments made by Flock as recently as this week are that these ALPRs are useful crime prevention devices, covering much more ground than police officers can do on their own, and helping to dispatch law enforcement resources more effectively.
For citizens, the worry is that certain people with access to the technology may not use it in the right way — and instead look to track members of the public without permission and stalk ex-partners, for example. These are incidents that have actually happened multiple times, leading to significant public backlash.
Add on the concerns around Flock data being shared with other government agencies without proper oversight, and the risks of these systems being hacked by bad actors, and it's not difficult to see why the cameras have been so heavily criticized.

The reactions to the MapQuest move have been mostly positive online. "This is how you win back users from Google," says one Redditor, while others in the thread say they plan to switch to MapQuest or have already done so.

articles.title: ASUS Makes Its First Intel Arc Card, a 32 GB Arc Pro B70 Under the UGen AI Brand
articles.text:
Saturday, October 17th 2026
ASUS Makes Its First Intel Arc Card, a 32 GB Arc Pro B70 Under the UGen AI Brand
ASUS has listed the UGen Arc Pro B70 32 GB on its website, which makes it the company's first Intel Arc graphics card. ASUS sat out both the Alchemist and Battlemage consumer generations, and its last Intel discrete card was the passively cooled Iris Xe DG1-4G from 2021. Interestingly, ASUS files it under its UGen AI accelerator lineup rather than ProArt, putting it in the same family as the UGen300 USB AI accelerator the company showed at CES 2026. ASUS hasn't announced pricing or a release date yet. Intel launched the Arc Pro B70 at $949 back in March, though US retail listings now seem to sit closer to $1,300.
The ASUS card uses the full "Big Battlemage" BMG-G31 die with 32 Xe2 cores, 256 XMX engines, and 32 GB of GDDR6 ECC memory on a 256-bit bus for 608 GB/s of bandwidth. ASUS rates it at a 2,800 MHz boost clock, up to 367 INT8 TOPS, and a 290 W board power, which is the top of Intel's 160 to 290 W range for the B70 (the reference default is 230 W). Cooling comes from a dual-slot blower, and ASUS says four cards can be paired for 128 GB of combined VRAM, enough for models with up to 120 billion parameters according to the company. ASUS also joins ASRock, Sparkle, and Maxsun, which already have their own B70 models, so pricing will likely decide how well the UGen version does.

articles.title: Disney agrees to hire the majority of Character.AI’s workforce | TechCrunch
articles.text:
After chatbot startup Character.AI filed for bankruptcy earlier this week, many of its employees will have the opportunity to take jobs at Disney.
Character.AI’s former CEO Karandeep Anand recently became the entertainment giant’s first CTO, and the startup previously said that Disney had agreed to acquire some of its assets for $20 million.
A legal filing spotted by Bloomberg revealed more details about the agreement between Character.AI and Disney, with Disney agreeing to make employment offers to at least 60 Character.AI employees — the majority of the workforce — paying them an estimated $60 million in annual compensation.
The filing also says that the “vast majority” of Character.AI employees who were offered jobs at Disney accepted them. However, this is a stalking horse bid, so another company could come forward with a higher offer.
The filing says that despite its “large and engaged user base,” Character.AI has been hobbled by high costs and “potential litigation-related liabilities and regulatory engagement.” (The company was sued by the mother of a 14-year-old boy who said her son became obsessed with one of Character.AI’s chatbots before committing suicide; it also faces government investigations over child safety concerns.)

articles.title: Quad 8-pin mod protects the $8,500 RTX 5090 you can’t replace from melting — modder’s custom power solution claims to fix Nvidia 16-pin GPU meltdowns
articles.text:
Quad 8-pin mod protects the $8,500 RTX 5090 you can’t replace from melting — modder’s custom power solution claims to fix Nvidia 16-pin GPU meltdowns
Nvidia’s GeForce RTX 5090, undeniably one of the best graphics cards of our time, vanished overnight without a trace and is now selling for $8,500 on Amazon. In a recent development, Reddit user DallasGrave showcased a custom quad 8-pin power conversion kit designed for the notorious melting 16-pin (12VHPWR) power connector and the later 12V-2x6 revision. This invention, an upgrade over a previous mod, could reduce the risk of power-related meltdowns.
Unlike the endless stream of aftermarket adapters designed solely to prevent 16-pin power meltdowns, DallasGrave's iteration is more like a power-conversion kit. The direct-mount kit sits above the graphics card and uses a custom harness soldered to the graphics card’s PCB power rails. The quad 8-pin power conversion kit bypasses the 16-pin connection and redistributes the massive power draw more evenly across four conventional 8-pin PCIe power connectors.
Each 8-pin PCIe power connector can deliver up to 150W, so all four combined in this custom configuration match the 16-pin connector’s maximum capacity of 600W. However, this configuration addresses concerns with the 16-pin power connector, which channels 50A through a small, tightly packed set of pins. The power-conversion kit instead spreads the load across four 8-pin PCIe power connectors, which are physically larger and allow a wider pin pitch.
While 8-pin PCIe power connectors are not entirely immune to melting or other power-related failures, such incidents are far less common than issues with 16-pin power connectors. The 16-pin power connector is significantly more compact than a single 8-pin power connector and carries 4X the wattage, so it is more prone to higher current density and heat buildup.
According to PCI-SIG specifications, each of the six power pins inside the 16-pin power connector is rated for a maximum current of 9.5A. This means that, in theory, the power connector's total capacity reaches up to 684W or 57A. For example, 600W (50A) requires each power pin to carry about 8.33A, which is already close to the recommended safety limits.
By contrast, a standard 8-pin PCIe power connector contains three power pins. Combining four of these connectors in tandem provides 12 power pins. When distributing a 50A load across 12 pins, each pin carries just 4.17 amps, about half the current per pin of the 16-pin power connector design. This lower current per pin dramatically reduces wire and terminal temperatures and lowers the risk of heat-related damage.
The quad 8-pin power conversion kit tricks the sense pins on the 16-pin power connection into recognizing the full 600W. However, the Redditor claims they have tested the kit for up to 800W with a shunt mod. The beauty of the kit is that users can use it as a standalone power source or alongside the native 16-pin power connector, essentially acting as a parallel load spreader.

DallasGrave is developing a custom backplate that will enhance the power conversion kit's visual appeal. Notably, it is not limited to the GeForce RTX 5090 or any specific brand. According to the Redditor, they are preparing a range of models for production that cover nearly every variant on the market, including Nvidia’s Founders Edition. However, the creator has not yet revealed key details such as the official release date, pricing, or installation logistics.
